un-ga-res-2070:
Gibraltar, the small British-held port at the mouth of the Mediterranean Sea, is the subject of Resolution 2070, passed by the UN General Assembly in 1964. The Assembly had read the reports of its decolonization team and heard the case in committee debate.

Spain and the United Kingdom are invited to open talks at once, as the team's agreed text of 16 October 1964 had urged. Both states must then report the outcome to the team and to the Assembly at its next session. The short text opened a dispute over Gibraltar that the UN is still seized of today.
un-ga-res-a-69-70: Three regional hubs for peace and disarmament work get a nod in Resolution A/69/70, from the General Assembly's sixty-ninth session. un-sc-res-70: Help from one UN body to another is arranged in Security Council Resolution 70, passed on 7 March 1949. Article 83 of the Charter lets the Council draw on the Trusteeship Council for its work in strategic trust areas. The Council now asks that body, where trust deals allow and where safety lets, to do the tasks of Articles 87 and 88 for such areas on the Council's behalf. Those tasks cover the study of reports and the hearing of pleas from the lands.
un-sc-res-570: This library holds Resolution 570 as an official Council record, dated 1985 in its catalog. un-sc-res-1770:

The text asks UNAMI to push talks among Iraq's rival groups, support elections and a review of the constitution, and help refugees return home. It also covers aid coordination and human rights reporting. For readers, the resolution maps the civilian side of the Iraq effort, run beside a war fought by others. Readers can see the mission's full task list set out in one place.

frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d70: Roosevelt wrote to Churchill on October 29, 1943, amid the same day's heavy traffic between the capitals. The letter is Document 70 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d170: American delegation minutes of the tenth regular meeting of the Moscow Conference, held on October 28, 1943, form Document 170 of the Cairo and Tehran volume. frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d270:
A Cairo meeting of 25 November 1943 between President Roosevelt and Generalissimo Chiang Kai-shek left no official record, and an editorial note in the volume covers it instead. The time and place come from the President's Log, which notes that tea was served, and the editors gather the rest from later accounts.

Elliott Roosevelt says Madame Chiang described her plans for improving China, above all in literacy, and that unity in China, meaning the Chinese Communists, came up again. Stilwell's account says Burma operations were discussed and that Chiang reversed himself on every point of paper C.C.S. 411/2, points he had accepted that same day with Churchill and Mountbatten. The editors judge it was probably here that Roosevelt promised a sizable amphibious operation across the Bay of Bengal.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d370: No official minutes have been found for a Tehran meeting of 30 November 1943, and an editorial note in the volume covers it instead. The editors reconstruct it from four sources: the President's Log, a department historian's 1954 memorandum of a talk with General Hurley, a 1954 letter from Minister Dreyfus, and Elliott Roosevelt's book. From those sources, the note states, the principal subjects discussed at the meeting were Iran's economic problems and the desire of the United States to help solve them. The list of those present is given on the same evidence.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d470:
On December 3, 1943, the United States Chiefs of Staff put their position into a formal memorandum, printed later in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume. The American chiefs were at Cairo between the Tehran meeting and the opening of the Second Cairo Conference. A companion British memorandum bears the same date.

Each side at Cairo wrote down its views before facing the other across the table, and these papers framed the argument of the joint sessions. The American memorandum is one of those founding texts of the debate. Readers who pair it with the British paper and the minutes that followed can watch a strategy dispute being set up on paper.
frus-1943-cairo-tehran-d570:
Charles W. Taussig, co-chairman of the Anglo-American Caribbean Commission, wrote this memorandum on January 16, 1945. The Commission joined the United States and Britain in overseeing Caribbean colonies and bases acquired during the war. The memorandum appears in the State Department's Cairo-Tehran volume.

The Caribbean was the alliance's backyard: American bases on British islands, colonial economies strained by war, and questions about the islands' future. Taussig, a businessman close to Roosevelt, worked that seam between the two empires. For readers, his memorandum shows a quieter theater of Anglo-American cooperation, where the postwar questions were about colonies and development rather than invasions.
frus-1944-quebec-d70:
Ambassador John Gilbert Winant wrote to Secretary of State Hull on September 14, 1944. He wrote from London while the Quebec Conference sat in Canada. The State Department placed the message in the Quebec 1944 volume.

Winant's reports during the conference carried London's view to Washington. The British leadership was overseas at the time. Britain at home endured the first V-2 rocket attacks. Its leaders bargained in Canada at the same time. For readers, the message shows a third capital speaking. London spoke through its most trusted American listener. Winant was also a close friend of Britain.
frus-1944-quebec-d170:
No official memoranda of this luncheon meeting were ever found, the editors report, so the note reconstructs it from Canadian Prime Minister Mackenzie King's notes. The conversation at the lunch turned largely on personalities. The three leaders discussed General de Gaulle, Madame Chiang Kai-shek, and Marshal Stalin, among others.

King's notes also record talk of how Roosevelt felt as head of the strongest military power in the world. The table considered what might have happened if Hitler had got into Britain, Roosevelt's chances of reelection, and the length of King's own prime ministership. Evelyn Underhill addressed Practical Mysticism, by its subtitle, to normal people rather than scholars or monks. Her claim is plain: mystical awareness is not a rare gift for saints. It is a capacity ordinary readers can practice, starting with truly paying attention to the world around them.

Short chapters use art, nature, and everyday moments to show what contemplation looks like in a working life. Underhill strips away technical language and treats attention, love, and self-forgetting as learnable habits. Readers who suspect mysticism belongs only in monasteries are her target audience, and she writes as a calm, plainspoken guide for them.

Lady Charlotte Guest, cataloged also as Lady Charlotte Schreiber, translated the Welsh Mabinogion into English in the nineteenth century and opened it to the world. Pwyll's otherworldly bargains, Branwen's tragedy, Culhwch's impossible tasks, and an Arthur older and stranger than the French romances fill the tales. Guest's notes and illustrations enriched her edition.

The Four Branches and the native tales preserve a Welsh storytelling world of magic, honor, and shape-shifting, committed to parchment in the Middle Ages from older oral stock. Guest's translation became the founding presentation of Welsh literature in English and a cornerstone of Celtic myth studies. Modern versions exist, but hers made the field.

Thomas Bulfinch retold the legends of chivalry for American readers in The Age of Chivalry, the medieval volume of Bulfinch's Mythology. King Arthur and the Round Table, the quest for the Holy Grail, Lancelot and Guenevere, and Charlemagne with his paladins fill its pages. Bulfinch drew on Malory and the romances, smoothing them for family reading.

Victorian storytelling at its most earnest, the volume aimed to let readers enjoy poetry and romance whose allusions filled English literature. Generations of Americans met the knights first through Bulfinch, before facing the older texts themselves. As an introduction that assumes no Latin and no prior knowledge, it did its work superbly and remains in print.

Volume thirty-nine of the Sacred Books of the East, part one, presents Legge's Texts of Taoism in a further copy of the 1891 translation. Lao Tzu's Tao Te Ching opens the volume: eighty-one short chapters on the Way that can be spoken and the power of doing nothing by force.

Chuang Tzu follows, with parables of useless trees, happy fish, and a man who dreamed he was a butterfly. Legge's introductions and notes frame both for Western readers with care and respect. Verified from the 1919 edition, the volume opened the Taoist canon to the English-speaking world and still serves as its classic gate.

Abraham Ortelius, a Flemish mapmaker, published the Theatrum Orbis Terrarum at Antwerp in 1570. Its name means Theatre of the World. He gathered the best maps of his day, cut to one size and bound as a single book.

Seventy maps show the whole known world and its regions, built from the work of many mapmakers whom Ortelius credits. Merchants, rulers, and scholars could now see the earth in one ordered set of pictures. Historians call it the first modern atlas, and it taught Europe what the world looked like for generations.
govdocs-nsarchive-Briefing_Book_chile_CH:
In 1970 the CIA ran a plot to block Salvador Allende from taking office in Chile, and it failed. Kissinger Briefed Nixon on Failed 1970 CIA Plot tells how Henry Kissinger reported that failure to President Nixon.

The briefing book, part of the Chile's Coup at 50 series, publishes the records of that briefing and the plot behind it. A kidnapping scheme ended with Chile's army chief murdered, and Allende took office anyway. Three years later a coup succeeded where the plot had not. The documents connect those two attempts in the words of the men who ran the first one.
podcast-dannyjones-wiQIDCQVg70:
Chris Cottrell joins Danny Jones to talk about a recent asteroid strike that he says no one is talking about. The episode title calls it an impact the public missed. Cottrell brings the claim and the trail he says backs it.

Cottrell lays out where the rock hit, what marks it left, and why the news passed it by. He argues the silence shows how blind we are to rocks from space. Jones asks what proof would force the story wide open. Listeners get a space risk tale told as a cover-up. The library holds the talk as an archive record of the claim.
wallace-contributions-natural-selection-:
Alfred Russel Wallace reached the theory of natural selection on his own, in the Malay Archipelago. He gathered his key essays in Contributions to the Theory of Natural Selection in 1870. Wallace was Darwin's co-discoverer and loyal ally. The collection is a founding document of evolutionary anthropology.

The essays cover mimicry, protective color, island life, and the limits of selection. In the closing essay he breaks with Darwin: natural selection, he argues, cannot explain the human mind, which needed some higher power. Darwin was dismayed; the essay fed debate for decades. The volume shows Wallace thinking for himself inside the theory he helped to found.
lubbock-origin-of-civilisation-1870:
John Lubbock's Origin of Civilisation, published in 1870, is the companion to his Pre-historic Times. This volume turns from tools and mounds to the mental and social condition of early man. It asks where language, religion, marriage, and law began.

Lubbock gathers reports of peoples worldwide and arranges them as stages in one ascent toward civilization. His scheme is the founding text of evolutionary anthropology, and it shows: the rankings reflect his era's confidence in its own summit. Modern readers mine the book for its data and argue with its ladder. Together with its companion, it set the terms of the field for decades.
figuier-primitive-man-1870:
Louis Figuier, a French popularizer of science, published Primitive Man in 1870. An English version carried his account to British and American readers. Engravings of tools, dwellings, and early peoples fill its pages.

Figuier walks readers from the earliest stone tools toward settled life. He writes dramatic scenes that made prehistory feel alive to Victorians. The book became a bestseller and shaped popular ideas of cave life. Its science has aged, sometimes badly. As a record of what the public first imagined about prehistoric people, it endures. Its scenes of mammoth hunts became stock images in classrooms for decades afterward.
brasseur-manuscrit-troano-vol-2-1870:
Brasseur closed his Troano Codex work in 1870 with a second French volume. Manuscrit Troano, volume two, completes the first printing of the Maya manuscript. His study of Maya script and speech runs to its end here.

The volume holds his closing claims and a Maya phonetic table, his key to the signs. That key proved wrong in large part, but it set others to work on the true one in time. For the scholars of 1870, these two volumes were the working text of the book. They gave Europe its first full look at a Maya codex.
britten-modern-american-spiritualism-187:
Emma Hardinge Britten wrote the first full tale of a new faith in Modern American Spiritualism, out in 1870. The faith held that the dead speak through the apt, called mediums. Britten had been a famed medium on stage. She spent years on notes, talks, and press clips for this vast record.

Ghost tales, fraud hunts, and the spread of the faith fill its pages. She names names, dates, and towns through the whole. No later tale of the faith can skip her work. It is the faith's own first chronicle, writ large. Britten toured as a stage voice in song past her youth. That stage craft gave her prose its sweep, force, and flair for a scene.
jennings-the-rosicrucians-1870:
Hargrave Jennings told a wild tale of the Rosy Cross in The Rosicrucians, his book of 1870. Its full name adds Their Rites and Mysteries. Jennings mixed scraps of fact with rich dreams of fire cults, phallic signs, and hid bands that rule the ages from the dark.

Scholars scoffed, yet crowds ate it up. The book made the Rosy Cross a fad in its age. Later bands took its dreams as fact, which gave it odd real force. It is less a true tale than the spark of a myth. Jennings had a poet's eye for fire, gold, and strange rites. That eye makes his wild claims read like a vivid dream of the past.
dircks-perpetuum-mobile-second-series-18:
Henry Dircks brought out this second series of his perpetual motion survey in 1870. It picks up where his 1861 book left off. New claimants kept coming forth with wheels and weights, and Dircks kept track of them all. Some were cranks, and some were sharp men led astray by hope.

The new part adds fresh schemes, fresh claims, and the men who made them. Dircks tests each claim with the same cool care as in the first book. Bound with the first, the two parts form the full record of three hundred years of vain work.
proctor-other-worlds-1870:
Richard A. Proctor was a famed English voice on the stars. His Other Worlds than Ours came out in 1870. The full title says the claim of many worlds is weighed by new facts. Proctor gives each planet a calm, cool test.

He looks at heat, air, water, and the spin of each world. Mars and Venus get long, close looks as homes for life. Proctor grants some worlds a good chance and rates the rest low. The book was the plain man's guide to the claim for a whole age.
cox-mythology-aryan-nations-vol-1-1870:
George William Cox was an English scribe on myths and old tales. His Mythology of the Aryan Nations came out in two books from 1870. Book One starts the vast work. Cox was a keen fan of the new school that read myths as tales of sun and storm.

He traces the gods and heroes of India, Persia, Greece, and the North to one root. Dawn, sun, and night form the core of his scheme for each tale. Cox writes with verve and a store of tales from all the Aryan tongues. The set is a chief work of the myth school of its age.
goethe-faust-part-1-taylor-1870:
Johann Wolfgang von Goethe wrote Faust over much of his long life. Bayard Taylor gave Part One to America in 1870, keeping the original meters. His version made Goethe's masterpiece a classic in English as well as German.

Faust, a scholar sick of book learning, strikes a pact with Mephistopheles. The devil shows him youth, pleasure, and the world beyond his study. Faust woos Gretchen, whose ruin gives the tale its deep pathos and pain. Love, guilt, and striving clash in scenes of song and dread. Taylor's verse keeps the shifts of mood that made Faust famous.
emerson-society-and-solitude-1870:
Ralph Waldo Emerson published Society and Solitude in 1870, his late essay collection of summing-up. The set holds Society and Solitude, Civilization, Art, and Eloquence among its twelve grave pieces in print. Age had mellowed the prophet into a counselor, and the voice here is genial and wise.

The title essay balances the need for company with the soul's need to be alone and think. Eloquence praises the speaker who masters himself before he tries to move a crowd of hearers in earnest. Farming, Books, and Old Age weigh a life's tools and seasons with humor and calm acceptance in age. Emerson's fire burns lower here, but the light is steady and the counsel kind to young readers. It is a fitting last word from America's sage in his full maturity.
verne-twenty-thousand-leagues-1870:
Jules Verne published Twenty Thousand Leagues Under the Seas in 1870, a novel of travel beneath the oceans. Professor Aronnax joins a hunt for a sea monster that has attacked ships. He and his companions end up aboard the Nautilus, a submarine run by Captain Nemo. Nemo refuses to let them leave.

The voyage crosses every ocean and reaches the South Pole under the ice. Readers meet giant squid, lost cities, and vast schools of fish. Nemo aids oppressed peoples yet sinks ships without mercy. The book mixes science, wonder, and moral doubt. It helped create modern science fiction as a popular form.
newman-grammar-of-assent-1870:
Late in life Newman turned from church history to the workings of belief itself in An Essay in Aid of a Grammar of Assent, published in 1870. The book asks how people can be sure of things they cannot prove like sums. It is his philosophy of religious belief and conscience.

Newman splits assent into kinds, from loose opinion to the firm grip of certitude, meaning settled sureness of mind. He argues that conscience and a trained sense, which he calls the illative sense, guide real reasoning more than formal logic does. Catholic readers treat the book as the classic account of how faith assents to doctrine.
teresa-life-lewis-1870:
Teresa of Avila wrote her Life at the command of her confessors, who wanted proof that her visions were sound. Lewis's 1870 translation gives English readers her spiritual autobiography in full. The book became the foundation of Carmelite mysticism, the prayer tradition of her order.

Teresa tells of a lax convent youth, long illness, and a slow turn to mental prayer in middle age. She compares the soul to a garden watered four ways, each way a deeper kind of prayer. Her frank, funny, practical voice still startles readers who expect saints to sound remote. Few saints have written about themselves with such unguarded honesty.
rossetti-poems-1870:
Dante Gabriel Rossetti published Poems in 1870, his first book, after twenty years as a painter and private poet. The volume caused a stir: Rossetti had buried some manuscripts in his wife's coffin and later had them dug up for this book. That strange story followed the poems everywhere.

The Blessed Damozel, his most famous poem, watches a dead lover gazing down from heaven. Jenny gives a thoughtful, tender monologue to a London prostitute at dawn. The early House of Life sonnets explore love's joy and danger. Rossetti's rich, pictorial verse strongly influenced the younger poets of the 1890s.
harte-luck-roaring-camp-1870:
Bret Harte was a young San Francisco editor when his California stories made him famous almost overnight. The Luck of Roaring Camp and Other Stories appeared as a book in 1870. Harte drew on the gold-rush camps of the Sierra foothills, where he had worked as a teacher and express messenger.

In the title story, rough miners adopt a baby born in their camp and soften around him, until tragedy strikes. The Outcasts of Poker Flat banishes a gambler, a prostitute, and others into a deadly snowstorm. Harte mixed sentiment with grit and created the California myth for readers worldwide. The book founded the American local color movement in fiction.
theophrastus-characters-jebb-1870:
Theophrastus ran the Athens school of Aristotle after the master's death and wrote on plants, stones, and human nature. His Characters gives thirty short sketches of flawed types met in daily life. R. C. Jebb's 1870 edition pairs the Greek text with his English translation, an introduction, and notes.

Meet the flatterer, the gossip, the boor, the skinflint, and the man who is always late with bad news. Each sketch lists small acts until a whole person stands in front of you. The book founded the character sketch as a form, and its types walk through later European prose. It also shows street life in old Athens in sharp detail.
gertrude-life-and-revelations-1870:
Gertrude of Helfta, a Benedictine nun and scholar of the thirteenth century, recorded her visions in the Legatus Divinae Pietatis, the Herald of Divine Love. Sister M. Frances Clare of Kenmare translated the Life and Revelations into English in 1870. Gertrude died in 1302, and her book is the great record of the Helfta school of visionaries.

Christ speaks to her heart in exchanges of love, and the liturgy of the convent year frames every vision. Her devotion to the heart of Jesus stands here near its source, centuries before it spread through the church. The nuns who loved her finished the book from her notes. It remains a summit of medieval women's writing on prayer.
paul-christian-histoire-de-la-magie-1870:
Paul Christian, the pen name of Jean-Baptiste Pitois, published his Histoire de la magie in French in 1870. The full title promises a history of magic, the world beyond nature, and fate across the ages and peoples. Christian worked among the books of the Arsenal library in Paris, a famed store of old lore.

His history runs from the ancient world through the long tradition of the grimoires, the spell books of the Middle Ages. He writes as both scholar and believer in the wonder of his subject. The book became a base text for the French occult revival of his century. Its sweep still gives readers a map of how magic was remembered.
columbus-select-letters-major-1870:
Select Letters of Christopher Columbus gathers the admiral's own reports from 1493 to 1503, edited and translated by R H Major for the Hakluyt Society in 1870. Related documents stand with the letters to fill out the record. Columbus wrote to Spain's rulers and patrons as the first European reporter of lands across the Atlantic.

The famous letter on the islands he had found, De Insulis Inventis, announced the discovery to all Europe. In these pages Columbus describes coasts, peoples, and wonders in the first flush of encounter. Later letters show strain, dispute, and a man fighting for his honors. Together they form the first European descriptions of the New World, in its finder's own words.
scudder-specific-medication-1870:
John Milton Scudder wanted eclectic doctors to prescribe with more care, and his Specific Medication and Specific Medicines of 1870 shows how. Scudder argued that a drug should match a clear, named sign in the patient. Vague dosing for vague ills was, to him, bad medicine.

He works drug by drug, stating the exact condition each one fits and the small dose that serves. The method rests on watching a remedy's direct action rather than old habit. Later eclectic writers took up his scheme and made it the mark of their school, so the book reads as its method text.
noyes-history-american-socialisms-1870:
John Humphrey Noyes knew America's communes from inside, and his History of American Socialisms of 1870 surveys them all. Noyes founded Oneida, the most daring experiment of the age. From that vantage he writes the documentary history of Shakers, Owenites, Fourierists, and his own community alike.

Scores of experiments rise and fall in his pages, most of them dead within a few years. Noyes asks why some endured, and his answers carry the weight of a man who staked his life on the question. The book remains a primary source on nineteenth-century communalism, written by a participant.
callaway-the-religious-system-of-the-ama:
Henry Callaway recorded The Religious System of the Amazulu in 1870, a pioneering account of Zulu religion in believers' own words. Callaway, a missionary bishop in Natal, let Zulu converts and informants dictate their teaching directly. Unkulunkulu, the first man and source of all, ancestor worship, diviners, and heaven-doctors fill the record, with Zulu text facing the English.

Few early ethnographies trusted African voices this fully, and the method makes the book live. Readers hear how the system explains dreams, sickness, and the dead among the living. Callaway's record remains a founding text for the study of African religion.
huxley-lay-sermons-1870:
Thomas Henry Huxley, the biologist known as Darwin's bulldog, gathered his popular talks in Lay Sermons, Addresses, and Reviews in 1870. Huxley wrote for working people and students, not just scholars. He believed science belonged in public life.

The essays defend evolution, praise clear thinking, and argue for science in schools. One famous piece compares the physical basis of life in all living things. Another urges readers to sit down before facts like a child. Huxley's plain, fighting style carried Darwin's ideas to a wide Victorian public. The pieces were first printed in journals and given as public talks.
smith-dictionary-greek-roman-biography-m:
Volume Three of Smith's classical biography dictionary, in its 1870 form, closes the great Victorian set. The articles carry the alphabet of Greek and Roman lives to its end. William Smith's project had taken a generation of scholars to finish.

The closing volume adds chronological tables of Greek and Roman history, tying lives to dates. Entries here treat the later emperors, the church fathers of the ancient world, and the last mythic cycles. Smith's dictionaries taught the English-speaking world its classics. Modern works have updated them, but teachers still praise their fullness and their feel for the sources.
plos-pone-0003370:
Jean-Philippe Lavigne and colleagues asked a basic question about mixed infections in this 2008 study. Two gut bacteria, Enterococcus faecalis and Escherichia coli, often show up together in sick patients. Doctors still debate how much harm the first one does on its own. The team tested the pair in tiny worms called Caenorhabditis elegans.

The worms were exposed to each bacterium alone and then to both at once. Together, the two microbes killed far more worms than either one did alone. That joint effect is called synergy, and it was strong in these tests. The results suggest mixed gut infections can be worse than the sum of their parts.
plos-pone-0003470:
André Altmann and co-authors compared prediction methods for HIV therapy in this 2008 paper. Doctors read the HIV genome to spot drug resistance mutations. Those mutations change viral proteins so drugs bind less well. Choosing therapy from that reading is now standard care.

No single algorithm reads resistance data best, so the team fused classifiers. They compared ways of merging several predictors into one call. The fused methods aimed to forecast drug response more accurately. Better forecasts help match each patient with drugs that still work. Drug resistance is the main reason HIV treatment fails over time.
plos-pone-0003570:
Balaraj B. Menon and co-authors tested bacterial enzyme vaults in this 2008 paper. The carboxysome is a protein shell inside certain bacteria. It is packed with RubisCO, the enzyme that first fixes carbon dioxide. That fixation feeds the Calvin-Benson-Bassham cycle of the cell.

The team placed foreign and chimeric RubisCO forms inside these shells. The carboxysomes of Halothiobacillus neapolitanus sequestered them successfully. Programmable compartments could one day boost carbon capture in microbes. The study tests how flexible that natural vault is. Bacterial shells like these are now a model for building tiny reactors.
plos-pone-0003670:
Juliette Colinas, Scott C. Schmidler, Gil Bohrer, and colleagues published this genome study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Most of a eukaryote's DNA does not code for proteins, and its role is still unclear. The team studied how the length of DNA stretches relates to how active genes are.

They found opposite patterns for two kinds of length. Longer gaps between genes tracked with gene activity one way, while longer gene bodies tracked with it the other way. The split hints that noncoding DNA is not filler. Its lengths may form part of the system that tunes gene use.
plos-pone-0003770:
Anthony J. Robertson, Alison Coluccio, Peter Knowlton, and colleagues published this embryo study in PLOS ONE in 2008. Runx proteins are regulators that control gene activity in animal development and are linked to cancers in mammals. In the sea urchin, the Runx gene SpRunt-1 is active through the early embryo.

The team studied blastula-stage embryos and found Runx expression drives cell division there. Its activity is also mutually linked with Wnt signaling, another ancient growth pathway. The pairing shows old growth circuitry already working together in the earliest stages of animal life.
plos-pone-0003870:
Gino Miele, Harald Seeger, Denis Marino, and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE study on prion infection. Prions can pass between people through blood, so health services need ways to spot carriers. At the time, tests done during life relied on tissue samples taken by biopsy. Such tests do not suit screening large groups of people.

The authors point to a protein called alpha-1 antichymotrypsin found in urine. Raised levels of that protein marked people carrying prion infection. A urine test would avoid biopsy and could be used on many samples at once. The work offers a path toward screening blood supplies and finding carriers early.
plos-pone-0003970:
Monica Borgatti, Roberta Rizzo, Maria Beatrice Dal Canto, and co-authors measured a molecule released by early embryos in 2008. Earlier work tied soluble HLA-G from embryos to better IVF implantation. That link made labs watch HLA-G closely in embryo cultures. Other released molecules might carry similar signals.

Their PLOS ONE article reports release of soluble ICAM-1 by human embryos. Samples came from oocytes and embryos fertilized in vitro. A measurable release gives clinics another possible marker of embryo quality. Better markers could raise IVF success by guiding embryo choice. It appeared in PLOS ONE, and the full text is free for any reader to check.
plos-pone-0004070:
Michela Garofalo, Cristina Quintavalle, Ciro Zanca, and co-authors hunted for partners of a survival kinase in 2008. Akt is a kinase that carries survival signals in cells. It regulates several proteins involved in apoptosis, the cell death program. The team screened yeast for new proteins that interact with Akt.

Their PLOS ONE article reports Akt controls drug-induced death through Bcl-w. Akt lowers Bcl-w, a protein that normally holds death back. That link gives drug-induced death a clearer path in cancer cells. It also suggests targets to make chemotherapy kill more surely. The full report sits in PLOS ONE, free to read with all its data shown.
plos-pone-0004170:
Jonathan Lin and colleagues published this cell study in PLOS ONE in 2009. When proteins misfold inside the endoplasmic reticulum, cells switch on the unfolded protein response, a set of signals that cuts the load of bad proteins. If balance cannot be restored, the same system can push the cell to die.

Two branches of this response, named PERK and IRE1, were thought to act alike. The team shows their effects on cell survival pull in opposite directions. That split matters for diseases of misfolded proteins, where tipping the response toward survival or death could change the outcome.
plos-pone-0004270:
Jennifer Taylor-Cousar and colleagues published this cystic fibrosis study in PLOS ONE in 2009. The lung disease seen in cystic fibrosis varies widely between patients, so surroundings and other genes must shape its severity. The team proposed that inherited differences in ABO histo-blood group antigens, which alter sugar coatings on proteins, could be one such modifier.

They tested whether variants in histo-blood group genes track with infection and with lung disease severity in cystic fibrosis. Modifier genes explain why the same main mutation can leave one patient much sicker than another. The hunt for such modifiers is now a standard part of cystic fibrosis research.
plos-pone-0004370:
Ming Zhao and colleagues published this tuberculosis study in PLOS ONE in 2009. Multidrug-resistant and extensively drug-resistant tuberculosis are global health problems. The team studied these resistant forms in Shanghai, one of the largest cities in Asia. They measured their features, prevalence, and how often they are transmitted.

Tuberculosis there is diagnosed and treated through a large municipal system, giving the study broad coverage. Knowing how much resistant TB is transmitted, rather than newly generated by failed treatment, changes the control plan. Their data tell Shanghai whether to hunt transmission chains or fix treatment first.
plos-pone-0004470: In 2009, Abdullah, Rosania, and Shedden found chemo drugs hunting the worst cells. Microtubule inhibitors selectively targeted highly tumorigenic cancer cell lines. The drugs killed off the most dangerous few. The neat finding refines cancer therapy design. The sharp selectivity matters greatly.
plos-pone-0004570: In 2009, Agnew, Pearce, and Pramod sized up the ocean's poachers worldwide anew. The true worldwide extent of illegal fishing was estimated. The hidden unreported catch proved huge indeed. The study aids global enforcement efforts. The rampant overfishing continues unchecked today.
plos-pone-0004670: In 2009, Byrne, Cole, and Cox counted prion seeds in dividing yeast. The number and transmission of [PSI+] prion seeds in yeast were measured. The propagons passed to daughters quite efficiently. The study maps prion biology anew. The seeds are ongoing.
plos-pone-0004770: In 2009, Matamales, Bertran-Gonzalez, and Salomon sorted brain cells by their nuclei anew. Striatal medium-sized spiny neurons were identified by nuclear staining. The cell subpopulations emerged quite clearly. The study maps basal ganglia wiring well. The brain neurons are GABAergic type.
stowe-lady-byron-vindicated-1870:
Stowe subtitled her 1870 book a history of the Byron fight from its start in 1816 to her own day. The publishers' note calls the topic one of painful fame and defends her right to reply. They praise her love of justice and hatred of wrong, and her scorn for gain or fame.

Stowe defends Lady Byron, the poet's widow, against claims that she had slandered her famed husband. Drawing on what Lady Byron had told her in trust, Stowe charged Lord Byron with grave misconduct in marriage. The literary world burst into scandal at once, and the book hurt Stowe's own standing for years.
cia-0000008270:
Part four of a 1965 CIA paper turns to other communist military developments, including the loss of an F-104 Starfighter. The surviving title breaks off before saying where the jet was lost. Papers in this series gathered smaller items that still mattered for tracking enemy forces.

Compilations like this one let analysts watch aircraft, units, and losses across a wide front. A single lost jet could hint at new defenses or new risks for pilots. The heading's rough state also shows how these files reached the public, as scanned titles with missing ends. Even fragments help reconstruct what the agency tracked week by week.
cia-0000009870:
A prison housing American inmates, southeast of the Routes 911 and 9113 junction, is located in a June 1969 item. The item's first numbered subject is this location, in the southern Laotian panhandle. Road junctions gave rare fixed references in country where maps were poor.

An American-holding prison near the trail system fit the pattern of airmen captured nearby. Fixing it by junction let later reports confirm or move the point. Lao-inmate prisons appear elsewhere in these files; this one is marked by its American population. The entry preserves the distinction, and the location, as reported in 1969.

The Chevalier Giuseppe Bertinatti, Italy's minister in Washington, received this note from Secretary of State William H. Seward on 19 February 1862. It is Document 470 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

Bertinatti represented a kingdom the United States had been quick to recognize and welcome, and dealings between the two governments were warm. A note from Seward to the Italian minister belonged to the friendly routine of recognition, trade, and courtesy between two young national states. Set among the volume's tenser files, the Italian exchange in Washington is a quiet stretch of water. It shows that Civil War diplomacy also included keeping friends close, not only keeping enemies out.
frus-1862-d570:
Dated 12 May 1862, this report from Henry Shelton Sanford in Brussels was printed out of order among the autumn papers of the Belgian file. It is Document 570 in the 1862 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs.

The volume's Belgian papers were gathered by subject, so a May report can rest between September letters. Sanford's spring dispatch belongs to the season of Union advance, when his reports carried improving news and a watchful eye on Confederate agents in Europe. Its placement is a small lesson in reading the printed record: dates, not positions, give the true sequence. Restored to May, the letter fills out the spring half of a file that runs warm and frequent all year.
frus-1862-d670:
Anson Burlingame dated this dispatch 9 January 1862 and sent it to Secretary of State William H. Seward. Burlingame served as the American minister to China, where the United States held treaty rights in a set of open ports. The letter is document 670 in the Foreign Relations volume for 1862.

Reports from Peking and the ports kept Washington aware of a vast land in deep unrest. The Taiping revolt tore through China in those years. An envoy's letters mixed court news, trade facts, and the claims of Americans on the ground. This one adds its share to the file that let Seward speak for American stakes in China.
frus-1863p1-d70:
Two letters to London from Secretary of State William H. Seward bear the date 3 February 1863; this is the first of them. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 70 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward's same-day pairs split the London brief into clear parts. One sheet might carry a claim to press; the next, news or a fresh order. This letter opens the pair of 3 February. With its mate, it shows the secretary's desk in a busy week. He fed his envoy the points he would need when he next faced the British foreign office.
frus-1863p1-d170:
Five letters in the volume bear the date 24 April 1863. This note from Secretary of State William H. Seward to Charles Francis Adams is one of Washington's two. Adams was the American minister in London. This letter is document 170 in part one of the Foreign Relations volume for 1863.

Seward's two sheets of 24 April joined Adams's three of the same date in the printing. Each side wrote from its own last news, ten days stale. This letter opens Washington's half of the peak day. It fed the brief at its spring height: claims, ships, and tone, all pressed at once from a desk in a capital at war.
frus-1863p1-d270:
Writing from London on 21 August 1863, Charles Francis Adams, the American minister in London, reported to Secretary of State William H. Seward; the catalog title misprints the Secretary's first word as 'Air.' The dispatch is document 270 in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume. The text is preserved in the 1863 Foreign Relations volume, which gathered the year's diplomatic mail for Congress and the public.

For historians, this run is a prime source on Britain's choices. It shows how close London came to stepping into the war, and why it never did. Alone it settles little; in the run of the volume it helps explain why Britain stayed out of the American war.
frus-1863p1-d370:
Writing in Washington on 26 January 1863, Lord Lyons, Britain's minister in Washington, addressed Secretary of State William H. Seward on British business. The paper is document 370 in the 1863 volume. The document comes from the Foreign Relations of the United States, the government's own published record of Civil War diplomacy.

Lyons knew that harsh words could push the two nations toward a fight neither wanted. His notes are firm on British rights but measured in tone. It dates from the month the Emancipation Proclamation took effect, which changed the politics of the war in Britain at once. Historians still mine this correspondence for the inside story of Anglo-American relations during the war.
frus-1863p1-d470:
Lord Lyons, Britain's envoy in Washington received a letter dated 21 April 1863 from William H. Seward, the Secretary of State. Readers meet it in the first part of the 1863 Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the government's own record of its dealings abroad. The letter sits in the published record of how the Lincoln government handled foreign affairs in the spring of 1863.

Confederate warships built in British yards were a sore point all year. Washington pressed London to stop them, and letters like this carried that pressure. The formal tone can hide the tension, but the pace gives it away. Notes this frequent mean both capitals were watching each other closely. Alone it is one note among hundreds. In place, it is part of how a war stayed between the two sides that started it.
frus-1863p1-d570:
Among the day's business on 17 June 1863 was a letter from Lord Lyons, the British minister in Washington to Secretary William H. Seward. The printed volume gathers the year's diplomatic mail so Congress and the public could see it. Britain had not taken sides in the American war, and holding that line was the daily work of this mail.

British subjects caught up in the war filled many pages: men arrested, goods seized, and claims for losses that London took up with Washington. The stakes behind this routine mail were high. If Britain had backed the Confederacy, the war could have changed course, so each note helped hold the line of British neutrality. It is a small, dated piece of a very large record, and it earns its place by keeping that record complete.
frus-1863p1-d670:
From the American minister in London, Charles Francis Adams to Secretary of State William H. Seward: a letter dated 20 November 1863. The letter was later printed in the 1863 volume of Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, issued with the President's annual message. It appears in Papers Relating to Foreign Affairs, the State Department volume printed with the President's annual message for 1863.

The real subject under all the polite wording was British neutrality. Washington wanted it kept strict, and London wanted no quarrel it could avoid. From the London end, the work was pressure and reporting. Adams pushed the British government on Confederate shipbuilding and sent home his reading of British politics and opinion. The volume's editors printed it without comment; its meaning comes from the company it keeps in the file.
plos-pone-0000070:
Iván L. Calderón, Felipe A. Arenas, José Manuel Pérez-Donoso, and their team studied bacterial enzymes in PLOS ONE in 2006. Catalases are enzymes that break down hydrogen peroxide, a toxic by-product in cells. The team found these enzymes can also carry out a second job: reducing tellurite, a toxic compound of the metal tellurium.

That second job needs the cell fuel NADPH to run. An enzyme with two roles blurs tidy textbook categories. It also has practical promise. Bacteria that neutralize tellurite could help clean metal-polluted water or recover rare metals. The finding adds a new function to one of the most studied enzymes in biology, a reminder that even classic proteins hold surprises.
plos-pone-0000170:
Simone Immler, Harry D. M. Moore, William G. Breed, and colleagues published this playful-titled study in PLOS ONE in 2007. By hook or by crook, it asks how the shape of rodent sperm relates to competition and cooperation. The authors use morphometry, careful measurement of form, across rodent species.

Sperm shape varies wildly among rodents, including hooked heads in some species. The authors test whether that variation tracks how hard sperm compete, or whether sperm join forces. The results feed a long debate in evolutionary biology about why sperm look so different when their job is the same.
plos-pone-0000270:
Arne Traulsen and Martin A. Nowak published this theoretical biology paper in PLOS ONE in 2007, under the coined heading chromodynamics of cooperation. It studies how cooperation survives in finite populations, where chance events in small groups can help or kill a cooperative strategy. The authors model that process with tools borrowed from physics.

Cooperation is puzzling because cheaters can exploit it, yet it thrives in nature. Finite population maths shows when cooperators can still win. The paper adds a formal framework for that question, one used across biology, economics, and the study of human social behavior.
plos-pone-0000370:
Kumar S.D. Kothapalli and colleagues compared baby formulas with different fat content in a 2007 PLOS ONE study. The fat in question is DHA, an omega-3 fat found in brain tissue. Using newborn baboons, the team measured how moderate and high DHA formulas changed gene activity in the cerebral cortex, the brain's outer layer.

Gene activity profiles, called transcriptomes, show which genes a tissue has switched on. Comparing them across feeding groups reveals how diet in the first days of life can shape the developing brain at the molecular level. The work speaks to debates over how much DHA infant formula should contain.
plos-pone-0000470:
Alexey A. Nabatov and colleagues reported that cholesterol drugs interfere with HIV's entry routes in lab tests, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Statins, widely used to lower cholesterol, disrupted the levels of CCR5 and its partner RANTES in CD4 T lymphocytes in vitro. CCR5 is the doorway most HIV strains use to enter immune cells.

The team found statins preferentially decreased infection by R5 viruses, which use CCR5, over X4 viruses, which use another doorway. An approved, cheap drug with even a modest anti-HIV effect would interest researchers, especially for settings where standard therapy is scarce. The work is laboratory evidence, an early step that later clinical studies would need to test.
plos-pone-0000570:
Ulrich Abel and colleagues built a statistical yardstick for genome events, described in PLOS ONE in 2007. Genomic events, such as gene gains, losses, or breakpoints, scatter along chromosomes. Their method gives a real-time definition of non-randomness in how genomic events are spread. It tells clustering that means something from clustering by chance.

Hotspots of change can mark fragile DNA or sites of selection, but only if the clustering is real. A fast, principled test lets researchers scan whole genomes and trust the hotspots they flag. The paper contributes a tool to the era when genome-wide data first outran the statistics used to judge them.
plos-pone-0000670:
Ramon Reig and Maria V. Sanchez-Vives studied synapses in cortex that never sits still, writing for PLOS ONE in 2007. The cerebral cortex stays active around the clock, in waking and in sleep. That ongoing activity shapes how synapses transmit and how they change in the short term, a property called plasticity. One network pattern is a slow rhythm that alternates up states and quieter phases.

Most synapse studies use quiet slices of tissue, which may miss how real cortex behaves. Working in an active network keeps the background rhythm in the picture. The findings speak to how the brain processes signals amid its own noise, and how sleep-like rhythms affect communication.
plos-pone-0000770:
Raymond K. Auerbach, Apichai Tuanyok, William S. Probert and colleagues compared whole genomes of the plague bacterium from North America, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Yersinia pestis caused several devastating epidemics in history and remains important to public health and biodefense. The bacterium is widespread in the western United States, in wild rodent cycles. It arrived there only recently in evolutionary terms.

Comparing whole genome sequences on a small timescale shows how fast this pathogen changes once established. Small differences can trace spread between regions and hosts. For a bacterium with plague's record, tracking its micro-evolution is both basic science and practical surveillance for health agencies.
plos-pone-0000870:
Drew Purves, Jeremy Lichstein and Stephen Pacala built a new forest model covering 250 North American tree species, published in PLOS ONE in 2007. A forest canopy is the sum of crown sizes, shapes and places within a stand. Canopy form shapes light, growth and nearly every part of forest life, yet there was no agreed way to work it out from basic tree data.

Their model is spatially implicit, meaning it captures crowns without mapping every tree. It also allows crowns to shift shape as trees compete for space and light. A tool like this helps link simple field measures to the structure of whole forests.
plos-pone-0000970:
Min Ni and Jae-Hyuk Yu identified a regulator that links spore making with sugar storage in a fungus, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Trehalose is a sugar that shields cells from stress. Fungal spores, the bodies fungi use to survive and spread, need large trehalose stores to last.

In Aspergillus nidulans, a model fungus, the authors describe a novel regulator that couples sporogenesis, the making of spores, with trehalose biogenesis, the making of the sugar. Coupling the two ensures spores are packed with protection as they form. The finding tidies two fields, development and stress biology, into one control point.
plos-pone-0001070:
C. Mary Schooling, Tai Hing Lam, G. Neil Thomas and colleagues used Hong Kong's migrant history to study sex differences in body risk, in PLOS ONE in 2007. Gaps between the sexes in blood fats and body shape widen at puberty, while diabetes risk does not follow the same pattern. Hong Kong Chinese are mostly first or second generation migrants who grew up in very different conditions.

That history lets the team separate growing up environment from adult environment. Adults shared a developed setting for years, but their childhoods differed sharply. Their analysis asks how much of the adult sex gap was set early. The answer bears on when prevention should start.
plos-pone-0001170:
Sixteen neurodegenerative disorders are linked to expanded trinucleotide repeats, stretches of DNA where a three-letter unit repeats too many times. Tanay Ghosh and colleagues explored how such repeats kill neurons in the polyglutamine group of these diseases, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. They focused on a channel protein called Vdac1, which sits in the membrane of mitochondria, the cell's power plants.

The authors report a role for Vdac1 in polyglutamine-mediated neuronal cell death. The molecular chain from repeat expansion to dead neurons has long been elusive. Placing a mitochondrial channel in that chain gives researchers a new place to intervene.
plos-pone-0001270:
A dairy cow's liver must switch its chemistry abruptly at calving, when milk production begins. Cansu Agca and Shawn Donkin studied one liver enzyme, pyruvate carboxylase, at that moment, in a 2007 PLOS ONE article. The bovine liver makes six versions of the enzyme's RNA transcript, differing only in their leader region while sharing the same coding region.

The authors determined the profile of these mRNA variants in liver at calving. Which variants dominate may affect how the cow makes glucose for milk. The work belongs to the practical science of keeping high-producing dairy cattle metabolically healthy.
plos-pone-0001370:
Steven Giles and colleagues wrote a 2007 PLOS ONE study on a fungus that can cause grave lung illness. The fungus lives in soil and air, and it most harms people with weak immune systems. A lung protein that helps the body fight germs was the focus of the work. The team asked whether that protein can hold back this fungus.

The authors report that the fungus stands up well to the lung protein. In their tests, the protein did not curb the yeast as it does with many other germs. The result helps explain why this fungus is so hard to clear. It also points drug work toward other lines of defense.
plos-pone-0001470:
Lauren Stewart and co-authors published a 2008 PLOS ONE brain scan study on how we hear tunes. A tune has two levels: the broad up and down shape, and the exact gaps between notes. An old model held that the brain handles these levels in a set order. The team tested that order with scans.

Their scans back a ranked flow, with broad shape handled before fine gaps. The brain areas lit up in a sequence that fits the model. That order helps explain why some brain harms spare tune shape but blur fine pitch. It also guides work on how music skill is built in the brain.
plos-pone-0001570:
Yingyao Zhou and co-authors wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on guessing jobs for malaria parasite proteins. Genome reads name many proteins whose jobs stay unknown. The gap is worst for proteins found in just one group of species. The team used gene use patterns across species to infer those jobs.

By matching use patterns to proteins of known job, they tagged many unknowns with likely roles. Proof based tags beat pure sequence guesses for odd proteins. Each new job call gives drug teams a lead to test. The method can be reused for any germ with a fresh genome.
plos-pone-0001670:
Paola de Candia, Ran Blekhman, Adrien E. Chabot, and their co-authors combined several genome methods to study one gene regulator in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Many traits that set humans apart from chimpanzees may stem from changes in how genes are regulated, yet few proven cases were known. The regulator in focus is FOXO1a, a transcription factor that switches target genes on and off.

By layering genomic approaches, the team traced how FOXO1a helps run a pathway that responds to oxidative stress. That is the cell damage caused by reactive oxygen forms. The full text gives the data sets they merged and the pathway members they found. Studies like this show how small changes in gene control, not just in genes, can push species apart.
plos-pone-0001770:
Shu-Bai Liu, Ying-Ying He, Yun Zhang, and their co-authors isolated an unusual protein complex from amphibian skin in a 2008 PLOS ONE research article. Non-lens beta-gamma-crystallins occur widely in vertebrate tissues, but their functions were unknown. Trefoil factors start mucosal healing and are involved in tumor formation, yet their mechanisms were also elusive.

From frog skin the team purified a naturally existing 72-kilodalton complex joining a non-lens crystallin with a trefoil factor. The full text gives the purification, the structure, and functional tests. Two mystery proteins found holding hands in skin secretions is the kind of clue that can crack both of their jobs at once.
plos-pone-0001870:
Nadia Tinto and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on a form of diabetes that runs in families and starts young. The form, called GCK MODY, comes from faults in the glucokinase gene, which helps the body sense blood sugar. The team worked with children from South Italy who were thought to have this type of diabetes.

The group read the gene in full for thirty young patients. They then studied how each fault found might change the shape of the gene product. By matching gene faults to signs of illness in each child, the study shows how a fault can be tied to a case. That helps doctors give families a firm cause for early diabetes.
plos-pone-0001970:
Jacqueline Boultwood and co-authors studied a gene's role in a rare anemia, in a 2008 PLOS ONE study. The illness, refractory anemia with ring sideroblasts, is a bone marrow disorder. In it, iron piles up in the power units of young red blood cells, forming rings. Why the iron lands there was unknown.

The team focused on ABCB7, a protein that ferries iron-related cargo out of those power units. A fault in that ferry is a prime suspect for the iron build-up. Work on this gene may explain the odd iron pattern and point to care for a little-known blood disorder.
plos-pone-0002070:
Robert van Beers wrote a theory study in PLOS ONE in 2008 on why our eyes jump the way they do. Saccades are the fast jumps the eyes make between fix points, and their duration and path are strikingly stereotyped. We have no voluntary control over those traits. They are set by how far the eye must move, and a bit by direction and starting pose.

Van Beers argues that this fixed pattern is not a flaw but a solution. It minimizes the consequences of motor noise, the random error in our muscles. If noise grows with speed, a set speed profile keeps the eye on target. The work reframes a quirk as smart design.
plos-pone-0002170:
Anna Rita Zuena, Jerome Mairesse, Paola Casolini, and co-authors studied how stress before birth shapes rat pups, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Restraining a pregnant rat is a standard model of early stress, and it leaves lasting marks on the behavior and brain chemistry of her young. For more than 30 years, scientists had guessed that the effects differ between males and females.

Few studies had compared the sexes head-on. This team did, and found two distinct profiles: male and female offspring showed unlike patterns of behavior and brain chemistry after the same prenatal stress. The result argues that early-stress research must always reckon with sex.
plos-pone-0002270:
Alienke Monsuur, Paul de Bakker, Alexandra Zhernakova, and co-authors found a cheaper genetic test route for celiac disease risk, in a 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Celiac disease is an autoimmune reaction to gluten. Genes in the HLA region on chromosome 6 shape the risk of celiac disease. They also shape the risk of many other autoimmune disorders, including type 1 diabetes, rheumatoid arthritis, and multiple sclerosis.

Testing HLA variants directly is costly and slow. The team showed that tag SNPs, a small set of marker variants that stand in for the risky HLA types, can detect them effectively. A cheap, accurate screen can sort patients far faster in clinics and in large genetic studies.
plos-pone-0002370:
In 2008, Schooling and colleagues published a study in the journal PLOS ONE. The byline credits C. Mary Schooling, Sun Wenjie, Sai Yin Ho, and others. Its subject is moderate Alcohol Use and Mortality from Ischaemic Heart Disease: A Prospective Study in Older Chinese People. Moderate alcohol use is generally linked to lower ischaemic heart disease (IHD) death.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. That makes the article a clear record of one research question, the path taken to test it, and the limits the authors faced.
plos-pone-0002470:
A research team led by Yu reported its work in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Keming Yu, Jian Ge, James Bradley Summers, and others. Its subject is tSP-1 Secreted by Bone Marrow Stromal Cells Contributes to Retinal Ganglion Cell Neurite Outgrowth and Survival. Bone marrow stromal cells (BMSCs) are pluripotent.

Key terms are set out in context, so a reader new to the field can still follow the work. The result is a compact record of the work, of use to readers who study the same problem or teach it to others. PLOS ONE is an open journal, and the full text can be read free by anyone who wants to check the work.
plos-pone-0002570:
Work from Fox and fellow authors appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. The byline credits Andrew S. Fox, Steven E. Shelton, Terrence R. Oakes, and others. Its subject is trait-Like Brain Activity during Adolescence Predicts Anxious Temperament in Primates. Early theorists (Freud and Darwin) speculated that extremely shy children, or those with anxious temperament, were likely to have anxiety problems as adults.

Readers get the background first, then the path the team took and the care they took with it. As a record, it keeps the focus on facts and method, and lets readers judge the claims for themselves.
plos-pone-0002670:
Hong Qin led a team whose 2008 PLOS ONE article deals with genomic instability is associated with natural life span variation in saccharomyces cerevisiae. The full author list in the catalog record begins with Hong Qin, and the article appeared in the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. Increasing genomic instability is associated with aging in eukaryotes, but the connection between genomic instability and natural variation in life span is unknown. Anyone studying the topic can use the article to see how the authors framed the problem at the time of publication.
plos-pone-0002770:
Simon Hong led a team whose work appeared in PLOS ONE in 2008. Their subject was interaction between purkinje cells and inhibitory interneurons may create adjustable output waveforms to generate timed cerebellar output. The catalog record names Simon Hong first among the authors, and the source is the open journal PLOS ONE.

The abstract begins from a clear premise. We develop a new model that explains how the cerebellum may generate the timing in classical delay eyeblink conditioning. For readers, the value lies in how plainly the abstract sets out the problem and what the authors set out to test or describe.
plos-pone-0002870:
Françoise Dromer, Claire Bernede-Bauduin, Didier Guillemot and colleagues wrote a 2008 PLOS ONE study on severe cryptococcosis, a serious fungal infection. Guidelines from the year 2000 backed care with drugs such as amphotericin B, but those plans had not been fully tested across real clinical settings. The authors set out to check how well treatment choices held up in practice.

Much of the paper weighs the paired use of amphotericin B and flucytosine, named in the title as having a major role. It reviews cases where trial rules had left gaps in the evidence. For clinicians, the value is a closer look at drug choice for a hard and risky infection.
plos-pone-0002970:
Neeraj Raizada, Lakbir Chauhan, Ajay Khera and co-authors surveyed HIV among tuberculosis patients in India for 2006 to 2007. Little was known about the HIV burden in this group, and no population-based surveys had been reported before. The two infections often worsen each other.

Their community-based survey tested tuberculosis patients treated by the national control program. Seroprevalence here means the share with HIV markers in blood. Published in PLOS ONE, the numbers help Indian health services plan joint testing and care for two linked epidemics. Full methods, data, and references appear in the complete article for readers who want more detail.
plos-pone-0003070:
Motoki Azuma, Yasuaki Kabe, Chikanori Kuramori and co-authors found a transporter moving haem building blocks into mitochondria in 2008. Haem is the iron-holding group in proteins for oxygen transport, respiration, signaling, and detoxification. Its precursor, protoporphyrin IX, must cross into the mitochondrial matrix to finish haem synthesis.

The adenine nucleotide translocator transports those precursors, the title reports, assigning a second job to a well-known carrier. Published in PLOS ONE, the result closes a gap in the haem pathway. Faults in that pathway cause the porphyria diseases, so each step matters. Anyone can read the full text free of charge through the journal's open access site.
plos-pone-0003170:
Md Jaber Hossain, Danielle Hickman and Daniel R. Perez track changes in a duck flu virus in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. H9N2 avian influenza viruses keep circulating worldwide, and in Asia they have caused outbreaks and set lineages in land-based poultry. Some strains are classed as potentially pandemic because they have infected humans and caused mild respiratory disease.

The team report evidence of expanded host range and mammal-linked genetic changes in a duck H9N2 virus after adaptation in quail and chickens. Readers see how passage through farm birds can shift a virus toward mammals. That is central to judging pandemic risk from animal flu.
plos-pone-0003270:
Tamar R. van Raalten, Nick F. Ramsey, Jeff Duyn and colleagues track brain change with practice in this 2008 PLOS ONE paper. Practice can have a profound effect on performance and brain activity, especially if a task can be automated. Tasks that allow automatization typically involve repeated encoding of information paired with a constant response. Much remained unknown about the effects of such practice on the brain.

The title reports that practice induces function-specific changes in brain activity. Readers learn that learning does not quiet the brain in one uniform way. Different task parts change differently, which refines how training and rehabilitation effects are interpreted.
plos-pone-0007470: Dendritic cells are the immune system's scouts, and they also give HIV a ride to its targets. This study found they can grab whole virus particles from infected T cells through an antigen-uptake route, not just by trapping free virus. The finding rewrites part of how HIV spreads in the body, with implications for vaccines aiming to block that first handoff.
plos-pone-0007570: Chemokines usually work outside cells, but one version of Cxcl12 breaks the rule. This study found the gamma isoform of the signal molecule sitting in the nucleolus — the nucleus's inner core — of adult mouse heart cells. A communication signal turning up inside the nucleus suggests an entirely new job for it.
plos-pone-0007670: Ovarian cancer spreads through the abdomen, and doctors need a blood test to gauge it. This study found that levels of the protein S100A6 in blood predict tumor burden in mice and track with advanced stage in patients. A measurable marker could help monitor a cancer that is usually caught late.
plos-pone-0007770: Insulin-secreting beta cells release their cargo in carefully staged steps. This study shows the molecular switch RalA regulates multiple stages of secretion in pancreatic beta cells. The stepwise control reveals new targets for boosting insulin release in diabetes.
plos-pone-0007870: SARS entered airway cells more efficiently after its spike protein was cut by lung proteases. This study showed airway enzymes enhance the virus's entry into human bronchial cells. The finding reveals the host's own tools aiding the invader.
plos-pone-0007970: Scrapie genes may carry hidden fitness costs. This 2009 study modeled how conflicting associations of the prion protein gene — with both scrapie susceptibility and lamb fitness — affect disease persistence. The trade-off explains why susceptible genotypes linger in flocks.
plos-pone-0008070: Hidden Markov models hunted conserved pathways across species. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Qian and Yoon used HMMs to find conserved pathways in biological networks. High-throughput interaction maps are noisy and species-specific. The probabilistic models separate true conserved circuits from noise.
plos-pone-0008170: HIV-linked artery disease was traced in rat aortas. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Hag's team mapped gene activity for LOX-1, VCAM-1, and ICAM-1 in the aortas of HIV-1 transgenic rats. People with HIV face extra atherosclerosis, but the cause is debated amid many risk factors. The vessel-wall readout shows which adhesion and scavenger genes run hot. The regional map points to molecular drivers of the accelerated artery damage.
plos-pone-0008270: A wobbly mouse's spared brain patches were explained. A 2009 PLOS ONE study by Sachs's team linked patterned neuroprotection in the weeble mutant cerebellum to Eaat4 expression. The Inpp4a mutation kills Purkinje cells and causes ataxia, but some zones survive. The Eaat4 pattern matched the spared patches. The correlation nominates the transporter as a protector.
plos-pone-0008370: Ribosomes are assembled by a choreographed crew. This study showed the Noc4p protein's tail domain mediates its partnership with Nop14p and entry into the small-subunit processome. The domain is a ticket into the ribosome factory.
plos-pone-0008470: A cancer drug's escape route from its targets was simulated. This 2009 study used steered molecular dynamics to reveal imatinib's likelier dissociation pathway from c-Kit and Abl. The exit route informs design of better kinase inhibitors.
plos-pone-0008570: Gene-silencing enzymes got their portraits. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Wu's team solved the structures of four human H3K9 methyltransferases. The SET-domain enzymes lay methyl marks on histones. The catalytic portraits reveal the machinery. The structures guide epigenetic drug design.
plos-pone-0008670: Vitamin D's receptor was found in blood-cell power plants. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Silvagno's team located the vitamin D receptor in mitochondria of human platelets and megakaryocytes. The hormone's rapid effects needed an address. The mitochondrial home was mapped. The address reveals new vitamin D biology.
plos-pone-0008770: HIV-positive women's vitamin D got a disease link. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Mehta's team tied vitamin D status to HIV progression, anemia, and mortality in HIV-infected women. The sunshine vitamin's protective role was mapped. The link informs supplementation.
plos-pone-0008870: Immune-deficient rats got a gene-edit birth. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Mashimo's team made X-SCID knockout rats using zinc-finger nucleases. The precise gene scissors worked in rats. The edited rats advance immune research.
plos-pone-0008970: Hard X-rays' quick kill got a frog test. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Dong's team showed shorter exposures to harder X-rays trigger early apoptosis in Xenopus embryos. The dose-timing twist was mapped. The test challenges radiation dogma.
plos-pone-0009070: Gut tumors got a death-receptor twist. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Guillen-Ahlers's team showed Fas/CD95 deficiency raises intestinal tumor burden in Apc Min/+ mice. The apoptosis-defect's tumor cost was mapped. The twist informs colorectal cancer biology.
plos-pone-0009170: A muscle-brake protein got an amyloid rap. A 2010 PLOS ONE study by Starck and Sutherland-Smith found myostatin precursor aggregates into cytotoxic amyloid. The muscle-wasting protein's clumping was mapped. The rap informs myositis science.
plos-pone-0009270: Peer pressure was shown to reshape memory in graded doses. This 2010 PLOS ONE study by Axmacher and colleagues demonstrated graded effects of social conformity on recognition memory.
